design: The original framework uses one graph encoder for both pathways. The separate variant assigns independently learned graph encoders to history and item fusion. A second control averages two independent encoders and shares that average across both pathways. The latter two models have identical parameter counts. The original uses 989,264 versus 1,864,496 parameters on MovieLens and 124,614 versus 155,750 on Amazon, approximately 47% and 20% fewer, respectively.
results: The original shared model has higher observed full-catalog means in both domains: 0.01776 versus 0.01676 on MovieLens and 0.04987 versus 0.04801 on Amazon. Its paired differences are +0.00100 [−0.00164, +0.00373] and +0.00186 [−0.00057, +0.00558], respectively. At equal parameter count, the shared-average control also has higher means than separate pathways, with differences of +0.00089 [−0.00208, +0.00372] on MovieLens and +0.00046 [−0.00269, +0.00383] on Amazon. Every interval includes zero, so these comparisons establish neither a ranking advantage nor equivalence. The direct architectural finding is the observed performance–size trade-off: the original sharing design uses fewer parameters while achieving slightly higher mean scores in these runs. All sampled-ranking intervals likewise include zero; the supplement reports every comparison.
discussion: The sharing study directly evaluates the connection between the history and item pathways. Retaining the original shared encoder gives the most compact of the tested designs and the highest observed full-catalog mean among the three sharing configurations in each domain. The equal-parameter control separates this observation from simply adding an encoder: its mean differences also favor shared representations, although the estimated effects remain uncertain. These results characterize representation sharing as a parsimonious architectural option under the tested protocol.
conclusion: E2E-PREF connects collaborative, temporal and content representations through a shared differentiable recommendation architecture. Its experiments show competitive mean ranking performance in the studied Amazon domain and identify contrastive learning as useful for sampled MovieLens ranking. Direct sharing comparisons show that the original design uses fewer parameters than separate graph pathways and achieves slightly higher observed full-catalog means in both domains, with uncertainty that prevents a superiority claim. The contribution is an integrated preference-learning design supported by reproducible evidence about ranking, representation sharing and component behavior.
